topics.body_html:
A necessary electrolyte with an older reference framework

Chloride contributes to extracellular fluid balance and acid–base physiology. The retained US reference for adults aged 19–30 is an AI of 2,300 mg/day and UL of 3,600 mg/day. These were derived largely from sodium chloride and equimolar sodium assumptions in the 2005 report, rather than an extensive independent chloride-outcome literature. National Academies sodium and chloride chapter, 2005

This history matters when reading the index: sodium's 2019 system now uses a CDRR and has no UL, while the retained chloride values originate in the earlier framework. They are not evidence that all nutrient limits were established by identical methods. The distinction should remain visible rather than forcing both electrolytes into matching minimum/maximum boxes.

What is missing from this record

The food catalog contains no chloride values for any of the thirteen logged foods. The attention flag is Clarify, a composition gap rather than a deficiency flag. Restaurant salt is unquantified, and the known sodium subtotal itself is incomplete.

It would be tempting to multiply sodium by a salt-based conversion and call that the day's chloride. That would assume all sodium came from sodium chloride, miss chloride associated with other salts, and still omit restaurant sodium. Such a conversion may describe a known quantity of table salt, but it cannot reconstruct this whole diet.

What would improve the record

If salt is added to ayran or food, record the quantity and product. That supports both sodium and chloride estimates from a known ingredient. A restaurant recipe could also help. A database comparator, if introduced, should retain its uncertainty and avoid turning missing values into zero.

The current log supplies no reason to add a chloride supplement. The physiological importance of an electrolyte and missing composition data are separate facts. Vomiting, major fluid losses or a clinically measured electrolyte abnormality would pose a clinical question beyond the food estimate; none is established by this record.

Research coverage here is limited to reference derivation and the interpretation of the missing data. No independent athletic benefit from supplemental chloride is claimed.

topics.body_html:
Why this reference deserves an explicit uncertainty label

The US system retains an AI of 35 µg/day for men aged 19–30, with no established UL. However, chromium's status differs from that of clearly essential minerals. NIH notes that the US reference was set in 2001 and has not been reevaluated by the Food and Nutrition Board. Later research questions whether chromium meets the criteria for an essential nutrient. NIH chromium fact sheet

In its 2014 scientific opinion, EFSA found no convincing evidence that chromium is essential and considered setting dietary reference values inappropriate. This is a substantive disagreement about the evidence, rather than two competing optimal doses. The website therefore preserves the US AI for transparent reference consistency while displaying its limited evidential footing. EFSA chromium reference opinion

What the food log can establish

Chromium is unquantified across every food in the current catalog. The attention flag is Clarify, referring to a database and reference-evidence gap, not a likely deficiency. It would be misleading to compare an invented zero intake with 35 µg and prescribe the difference.

Food chromium is difficult to measure reliably and can be affected by contamination during processing and analysis. The current diet should not acquire new foods merely to optimize an unreliable chromium column. NIH food-source limitations

Supplement research does not establish a dietary requirement

A randomized, double-blind study in 19 healthy older adults tested 1,000 µg/day chromium picolinate for eight weeks. It found no significant improvement in insulin sensitivity, serum lipids or body composition. The small and older population limits inference, but it provides direct counterevidence to broad claims that chromium supplements reliably improve body composition in healthy people. Amato et al., 2000

An earlier trial in 180 people treated for type 2 diabetes reported improvements in glucose and insulin measures with pharmacological chromium doses. That population and intervention address a different question from ordinary nutrition in a person without a reported diabetes diagnosis. Positive disease-treatment results do not resolve chromium essentiality or establish an athletic benefit. Anderson et al., 1997

The interpretation is deliberately restrained: pharmacological effects, if present in selected circumstances, do not make a missing dietary total evidence of deficiency. These study doses are descriptions of experiments rather than a proposed regimen.

What would change the decision

No chromium supplement was reported. The practical default is to keep varied, enjoyable foods and retain this field as unknown until credible composition evidence is available. A marketed chromium-containing product would require a separate review of purpose, dose, study population and interactions. No UL was set because data were insufficient; that does not prove high-dose safety. NIH excess-intake and medication sections

topics.body_html:
Role and ordinary references

Molybdenum supports a cofactor used by enzymes including sulfite oxidase and xanthine oxidase. The US adult RDA is 45 µg/day, with a UL of 2,000 µg/day from all sources. The upper value relies substantially on animal evidence because human excess-intake studies are sparse; it should not be treated as a desirable dose. NIH molybdenum fact sheet

Unknown is the correct current total

Every logged food has an unquantified molybdenum value. The attention flag is Clarify, referring to missing composition evidence, not to a likely deficiency. Dairy, grains, nuts and other foods can supply molybdenum, but the current catalog cannot quantify a brand-specific daily amount.

Replacing these unknowns with zeros would manufacture a deficit. Importing a generic comparator without marking its food match would conceal the uncertainty. Neither is an improvement over an honest blank value.

How much attention is useful

NIH describes dietary deficiency as exceptionally rare; an acquired case was reported in a patient receiving molybdenum-free total parenteral nutrition. Rare inherited molybdenum-cofactor disorders are different from low ordinary food intake. These contexts do not make this mixed-food pattern a demonstrated deficiency risk. NIH molybdenum deficiency discussion

A richer food-composition database could reduce the information gap, but there is no reason here to add a molybdenum product or restore disliked beans just to make this column computable. The useful work is to preserve the unknown and resolve it only with credible data or a material dietary/clinical change.

Evidence boundary

This dossier reviews requirements, the data gap and the rarity of ordinary dietary deficiency. It does not establish a clinical status measurement or a performance benefit from supplementation. No such benefit is claimed. A product advertised for detoxification or metabolism would require evidence for that specific intervention, rather than relying on molybdenum's biochemical role as proof.

topics.body_html:
Essential functions, uncertain individual requirement

Choline contributes to cell membranes, acetylcholine and methyl-group metabolism. The male adult AI is 550 mg/day and the UL is 3,500 mg/day from all sources. An AI is used because evidence does not define an RDA; a small daily difference from 550 mg is not a deficiency test. High intake can cause adverse effects, including fishy odor and low blood pressure. NIH ODS: choline

In a controlled depletion/repletion experiment, 57 adults were fed very little choline for up to 42 days. Many developed liver or muscle abnormalities that improved with repletion, with substantial differences by sex and individual characteristics. The study demonstrates a requirement for dietary choline. Its severe depletion diet does not show that an ordinary mixed diet just below the AI causes the same outcome. Fischer et al., 2007

What the latest log suggests

My food-log estimate is 535 mg, with a saved portion sensitivity of 500–605 mg. Generic chicken contributes about 197 mg, the confirmed whole yogurt tub 138 mg, a generic sardine comparator 60 mg and four bananas 46 mg. Brand-specific choline is unavailable, so the apparent precision should not drive a supplement decision. The eating date is unconfirmed; report recorded October 10, 2026.

Attention: No change indicated from this estimate. It is near the AI within ordinary portion and composition uncertainty. No clinical deficiency, liver abnormality or cognitive symptom has been established.

Eggs are an optional food, not a compulsory addition

A large cooked egg is an efficient choline source, approximately 147 mg in the NIH food table. It can replace another food when appealing, rather than increase an already large daily list. Chicken, fish and dairy already contribute choline. There is no need to add eggs merely to close a modeled 15 mg gap. NIH food sources

I reported preferring raw eggs, but an organic or Trader Joe's label does not by itself verify pasteurization. For uncooked use, select a product explicitly treated to destroy Salmonella; US refrigerated eggs and egg products require appropriate refrigeration. For immediate eating without storage, a cooked serving bought ready to eat is simpler. FDA egg safety

A small human tracer study found cooked egg protein more digestible than raw protein. Its five ileostomy patients limit the exact percentage's generalization, but it provides no nutritional advantage for choosing raw eggs. Evenepoel et al., 1998

Cognition claims need their own evidence

Being a precursor of a neurotransmitter does not show that extra choline improves cognition in someone already supplied. NIH describes inconsistent intervention evidence and no clear general cognitive benefit for healthy adults. Choline supplements, citicoline and alpha-GPC are different exposures; their claims should not be assigned automatically to eggs or this food estimate. NIH evidence review

topics.body_html:
Food cholesterol is not a blood test

Cholesterol supports membranes and hormone production, and the body synthesizes it. No dietary RDA, AI or UL is established. The 300 mg label Daily Value is a labeling reference, not a current personal intake boundary or a blood cholesterol concentration. An estimated food total cannot establish LDL, HDL, ApoB or cardiovascular risk. FDA label reference

The American Heart Association's dietary-cholesterol advisory emphasizes the overall food pattern rather than an isolated gram target. It does not imply that all amounts have no effect. Animal foods often vary in saturated fat and other characteristics alongside cholesterol, making food associations hard to separate. AHA advisory,2019/2020

Human evidence is mixed by outcome

A 2015 synthesis included 19 intervention trials with 632 participants alongside cohort studies. Trials found a modest average rise in LDL with higher dietary cholesterol, but studies were heterogeneous and did not settle long-term cardiovascular disease risk. This supports rejecting both “dietary cholesterol never affects blood cholesterol” and a claim that one day's food figure predicts an event. Berger et al.,2015

The 2026 dyslipidemia guideline continues to emphasize dietary pattern and health behavior in cardiovascular prevention. Its clinical decisions use measured lipids and individual risk, not this site's food-label percentage. ACC/AHA 2026 guideline

What the latest log contains

The model for my food log estimates 309 mg, with about 266–398 mg across saved portion scenarios. Estimated chicken supplies 263 mg, the sardine label 30 mg and provisional whole-tub yogurt 16 mg. Chicken edible weight is the largest uncertainty. The eating date is unconfirmed; report recorded October 10, 2026.

Attention: No change indicated solely because the estimate crosses the label's 300 mg. Blood lipid and family-history context are unreported. If a repeated dietary change or measured lipid finding later warrants action, review the whole pattern, saturated-fat sources and suitable food substitutions rather than diagnosing from this subtotal.

Practical choice

Fish and chicken have useful nutritional roles and can remain in the preferred pattern. Eggs may be included as a food choice, but should be logged if eaten and need not be added on top of all existing proteins. A tolerable smaller chicken serving may reduce both calories and cholesterol if meal size is a problem; there is no established need to make that change from the current cholesterol figure alone.

topics.body_html:
Three quantities that must stay separate

ALA is an essential plant omega-3. Its adult male AI is 1.6 g/day; no UL is established. EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 s found in oily seafood and algae. The US reference system has no separate RDA or AI for them. Conversion from ALA to EPA and DHA is limited, so walnuts and fish supply different useful forms. NIH ODS: omega-3 references and forms

A product's total omega-3 claim may encompass several fatty acids. It cannot be relabeled as EPA plus DHA without a verified breakdown, or added to EPA/DHA estimates from the same fish as though these were different nutrients consumed.

What the latest log contains

The latest estimate for my food log is 1.53 g ALA from available values, mainly 1.36 g from the assumed 15 g walnuts. Its portion sensitivity is about 1.25–1.80 g, and ten foods lack an exact ALA value. A partial estimate slightly below an AI does not establish inadequate intake.

The sardine label reports 1.74 g total omega-3 per can. The table separately contains about 0.41 g EPA and 0.53 g DHA for the day, primarily from a generic sardine comparator whose exact match to the skinless, boneless product is unverified. These are useful provisional composition estimates, not an analyzed split of this can. The report was recorded October 10, 2026; eating date unconfirmed.

Attention: Clarify the product breakdown; no increase indicated from this log. Keep the exact label total visible and the comparator clearly marked. A manufacturer EPA/DHA specification would improve the record. Do not double-count them.

Food choice and supplement evidence

Walnuts fit the reported taste preference. An enjoyable small oily fish with modest sodium is a practical source of marine omega-3 s. Compare sodium for the whole drained can, ingredients and flavor; fish oil capsules are not necessary simply because the EPA/DHA split is missing.

In VITAL, 25,871 older adults received marine omega-3 or placebo for a median 5.3 years. The primary combined cardiovascular outcome was not significantly reduced (HR 0.92; 95% CI 0.80–1.06), nor was invasive cancer. Some secondary outcomes, including myocardial infarction, were favorable. This mixed result does not justify claiming that routine supplements prevent all cardiovascular disease, and the population differs from a young training adult. Manson et al., 2019

The formulation and outcomes investigation examines high-dose prescription trials separately. Their patient groups and formulations do not establish my need for treatment.

topics.body_html:
Useful stimulant, not a required nutrient

Caffeine can improve alertness and some exercise performance, but has no nutritional RDA or minimum. The FDA cites 400 mg/day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects for most adults. EFSA distinguishes up to 200 mg in one dose from up to 400 mg spread through the day for healthy adults. These are population safety assessments, not goals or guarantees against anxiety, palpitations or disturbed sleep. FDA: caffeine, EFSA: dose and timing

What is known about this day

I reported owning 200 mg capsules, not taking a confirmed dose. The latest food table has 0 mg in foods with available caffeine data; that is not evidence of zero caffeine from all sources. Capsule use, coffee, tea, matcha, cocoa and timing remain unreported. The food report was recorded October 10, 2026; its eating date is unconfirmed.

Attention: Clarify. Record capsules actually taken, all caffeinated drinks and approximate times. One 200 mg capsule is about 2.6 mg/kg at the reported 77 kg; two total 400 mg before any drinks, and two together would exceed EFSA's single-dose amount. Do not turn the owned product into an automatic daily habit.

Performance and sleep belong in the same decision

Research summarized by NIH often tests 2–6 mg/kg before exercise, with benefits differing by task and person. This is a research dosing range, not a recommendation to take its top end. For a 77 kg person, that upper end would exceed the FDA's general daily amount. More is not a requirement for an effective workout. NIH ODS: exercise supplements

A randomized crossover study of 23 young men compared placebo with 100 or 400 mg taken 4, 8 or 12 hours before bed. The 400 mg dose affected some objective sleep measures even at 12 hours; fragmentation was greater nearer bedtime. The 100 mg dose had no significant average effect in this small sample. It did not test a 200 mg capsule, so it cannot promise an exact cutoff for me. Feeling that sleep was fine also did not reliably capture every objective change. Gardiner et al., published online 2024 / Sleep 2025

For late gym sessions, protecting sleep may be more valuable than an optional stimulant. Prefer earlier use if caffeine is useful, and adjust against actual sleep and symptoms. Tea or coffee can be chosen for taste, but count their caffeine alongside capsules; switching the source does not remove the stimulant exposure. Relevant conditions, medications and individual sensitivity are unreported.
